title: Kufic, Naskh, Thuluth
hook: angular, round, grand: the main scripts

segments.voice: Yesterday, khatt, the art of the reed pen. Your line was: beautiful writing. What did you write by hand slowly, and did it look different? Day one thousand four.

Say your own name three ways. First as a sergeant would bark it across a parade ground: clipped, square, every edge hard. Then the way a friend says it across the kitchen table: easy, round, clear. Then the way an announcer would call it into a stadium: long, rising, filling the whole space. Same name. Three voices. Arabic calligraphy works like that. The same holy words can be written in different scripts, and each one speaks in its own voice. Today: Kufic, Naskh and Thuluth.
screen: `ONE NAME, THREE WAYS.` → `CLIPPED, ROUND, RISING.` → `SAME WORDS, THREE VOICES.`

segments.voice: Kufic first. Its name, tradition says, comes from the city of Kufa in Iraq. Kufic is angular: straight strokes, sharp corners, letters stretched long along the line. It looks carved even when it's written in ink, and it carves beautifully, into stone, into wood, into the borders of buildings. Builders even laid it out in bricks and tiles as square Kufic, the letters turned into a maze of right angles, so that a wall could spell a name of God over and over. Kufic is the voice of the inscription: firm, monumental, a little stern. Naskh is the friend at the table. Its letters are rounded and even, with small, clear shapes that the eye reads quickly. It became a script for books, for copying the Qur'an to be read. Naskh is the voice that wants to be understood. Thuluth is the announcer. Tall uprights, wide sweeping curves, letters that climb over one another and interlace, often stacked in layers. It takes room. It is written large, for the headings of Qur'an chapters and across the walls and domes of mosques, where it is meant to be seen from below and from far away. Thuluth is the voice that fills the hall. So take one short line, "Say: He is Allah, the One!" In Kufic it stands like a gate. In Naskh it reads like a letter. In Thuluth it rises like a call. Each script a voice.
screen: `KUFIC: ANGULAR, CARVED, FIRM.` · `SQUARE KUFIC: A MAZE OF BRICKS.` · `NASKH: ROUND AND CLEAR, FOR READING.` · `THULUTH: TALL, SWEEPING, FOR WALLS.` · then, large: `EACH SCRIPT A VOICE.`

segments.voice: The practice: compare two scripts. Take a pen and paper. Settle, and breathe. Write one short word, your own name if you like, in straight lines only: no curves, all corners, like Kufic. Then write the same word again, round and easy, like Naskh. Go slowly. Put the two side by side and look. Which one sounds louder? Which one sounds kinder? Which would you carve over a door, and which would you write in a letter? The bell holds the time.
Kufic. The angular script, tradition says named for Kufa, carved in stone and built in bricks. Beside it, Naskh, round, and Thuluth, grand. Today's word.
Your line: each script a voice. Today, look up one image each of Kufic, Naskh and Thuluth, and see if you can tell them apart before reading the labels. Day one thousand four.

howItsDone: Calligraphers learn the classical scripts one by one under a master, using Naskh for readable texts and Thuluth for large panels and inscriptions, while Kufic and square Kufic appear in carving, tilework and brick.

fork.reveal: Thuluth is written large for mosque walls and domes, meant to be seen from below and far away.
